subject: penguin
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module that builds a standing penguin model using the SDK's joint, chain, part, sweep, and paint helper functions, aiming for roughly human-scale proportions and keeping the implementation safe and reasonably compact.

I'm sketching the body geometry using a lathe shape for a rounded egg-like torso, with the spine joint controlling position, and planning to apply countershading so the back is black and the belly white, plus orange accents for the beak and feet. I'm working through the lathe profile coordinates to get a believable rounded silhouette from feet to head.

For the head, I'll use a separate black sphere overlapping the top of the body, and I'm now mapping out the joint hierarchy -- hips as root, then a neck joint feeding up to the head -- to keep the rig simple while still letting the shape read clearly as a penguin.

For the beak, I'm thinking through how to orient cone-shaped upper and lower jaw pieces relative to the head joint, using local direction helpers like forward/up so the orange beak points outward correctly regardless of the joint's own axis conventions.

I'm reminding myself to keep the overall rig simple rather than over-jointing the model, planning hips as a root near body center with short legs and feet near ground level.

For legs, I'll build them as short chains between hip and ankle joints with flattened orange boxes for feet positioned in model space relative to the leg bone. Flippers can be set up similarly as their own wing chains attached off the body.

For the flipper shape itself, I'm realizing a tube extrusion won't give a flat paddle look, so I'll switch to an extrude approach instead — drawing a leaf-shaped profile in the side view and sweeping it forward with a thin thickness, placed at the shoulder joint.

Defining the flipper outline points...

For the flipper bone I'm setting the joint at the shoulder with the wing angled slightly outward and downward, using a sign factor so left and right flippers mirror correctly. Now I'm moving on to building the feet geometry as boxes positioned under the body.

For the body, I'm shaping it as a lathe profile anchored at the hips joint, working out the right coordinates so the belly bottom sits just above the floor while the feet touch down, and defining the egg-shaped profile points from bottom to top with mild smoothing to avoid self-intersection. I'm also thinking through the countershading logic—black on the back, white on the belly—based on surface normal direction.

That region's covered by the head sphere regardless, so I don't need extra geometry there. For the head itself, I'll place a black sphere atop the body joint, overlapping slightly where the neck meets the torso, and set up a head joint parented to the hips with an upward direction for aiming. Now I'm considering a white face patch, since Emperor/King penguins have distinct facial markings.

Rather than add decal textures, I'll try painting the white cheek patches directly onto the head sphere using a normal-based condition, targeting the sides where the x-normal magnitude is large.

For the eyes, I'm positioning small spheres using the head's local coordinate system with forward/left/up offsets, though I need to figure out how to mirror left/right since negative scaling isn't directly available as a word.

Still working out the left/right helper logic...

For the eyes I'll place a white sphere at the eye point and a small dark pupil sphere offset slightly forward, keeping the geometry simple rather than overly detailed.

Checking the distances confirms the eye spheres sit inside the head but protrude outward correctly, and the pupil placement is similarly fine. Now I'm adding a beak cone positioned forward and slightly down on the head, pointing straight ahead.

For a more penguin-like mouth, I'm thinking of splitting it into an upper beak and a lower jaw joint, with the jaw attached to the head near the mouth so it can open and close while keeping the head's orientation by default.

Now for legs, I'm setting up a chain joint "legL" parented to the hips, using a catmull path that curves down from the hip area to the foot, keeping in mind the body's bounds so the legs emerge visibly below the torso.

I need to raise the body's bottom edge so the legs aren't fully hidden — adjusting the body lathe profile to span roughly 0.08 to 0.72 in height, with the hips root placed at [0, 0.42, 0]. I'm refining the lathe curve points to give the body a rounded penguin shape, aiming for a total height near 0.75 which matches a realistic penguin proportion.

Checking the head placement at y=0.6 with radius 0.125, the top comes to about 0.725, nicely nested within the body's upper taper so the head sphere sits naturally without poking through oddly.

For the legs, I'm repositioning the hip joints inward to x=±0.1 at y=0.28 so they start tucked inside the body's radius at that height, then run down to around y=0.03. Checking the body radius at various heights confirms the legs stay hidden until they emerge near the bottom around y=0.08, giving short stubby legs peeking out — which matches the stylized penguin look I'm going for.

For the feet, I'm placing small orange boxes at the leg bottoms, and defining the leg sweep using a two-joint chain with a tapered radius. Now I'm checking the flipper placement at the shoulder joint — positioned at x=0.15, y=0.5, which sits just inside the body's radius there, and tracing how the flipper outline extends downward to see if it clears the body's tapering profile without clipping through.

Since the flipper needs to sit outside the body surface, I'm nudging its position outward to x=0.17 and considering whether to tilt its orientation vectors so it angles slightly away from the torso, but deciding to keep it simple and let it hang straight down like a natural penguin flipper.

I'm defining the flipper outline as a tapered shape with a sharp point at the tip, giving it thin black coloring with a slight bevel, then attaching it to the hips via a named wing joint so the shoulder position and orientation derive automatically from the parent. I'm also considering adding a small black cone as a tail nub near the back of the hips for extra realism.

For the body's belly patch, I'm thinking of painting it white where the front-facing normal exceeds a threshold, giving the classic penguin chest look, and I'm exploring a smoothstep-based blend between black and white for a softer transition instead of a hard cutoff.

I'm settling on colors—dark charcoal black, warm off-white, orange beak, and pure white/black for the eyes—and deciding to bump up lathe segments for smoother curves given the small scale of the model. For the head, I'm adding a cheek patch painted white based on normal direction to mimic the eye-ring marking seen on species like the Adélie penguin.

Now I'm beginning to draft the actual module, starting with imports for the builder utilities and types needed to construct the geometry.

I'm defining color constants for black, white, and orange, then sketching out the build function with a joint for the hips and a belly paint function that distinguishes white from black based on surface normal position.

Now I'm typing the body profile as an array of OutlinePoint tuples and lathing it around the hips bone with paint coloring, then adding a head joint parented to the hips with its own sphere geometry positioned above the body.

For the eyes, I'm defining a helper that converts a side value into a left/right offset so I can mirror sphere eyes and smaller pupils across both sides of the head using local coordinates. Now I'm setting up the beak with a cone geometry positioned using the head's local offset, continuing to work out its direction vector.

Adding jaw joint and lower beak...

I'm fixing the leg chains' naming conflicts, using a side-based template for hip/ankle joint names, and setting up the catmull path points for each leg. Then I'm sweeping the orange leg geometry and attaching foot boxes to the ankle joints.

For the foot attachment, I'm working through which joint index correctly represents the ankle tip, deciding to name three joints per leg chain (hip, knee, ankle) so the last joint in the array reliably gives the tip position for the foot bone.

Now I'm setting up the foot box geometry with its flat bottom resting at ground level, then moving to define leg radius tapering from hip to ankle, and sketching out flipper construction with an extruded outline, tapered thickness from tip to base, beveled edges, and black coloring bound to the wing joint.

Working through flipper placement relative to the body's curvature, naming the wing bones by side, then adding a small cone-shaped tail angled back and down from the hips, positioned so it sits naturally against the body's rear edge. I'm also checking eye placement on the head and making sure the white belly and feet don't awkwardly overlap before finalizing and returning the root bone.

Double-checking the hips joint hierarchy, leg sweep paths staying within the body radius, and the lathe/head paint functions that color surfaces white or black based on normal direction to create the belly and cheek patterns. Everything looks consistent, so I'll finalize the code with the proper exports and build function.
